entries.title: ‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’
entries.summary: Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her careerA few years ago, when Helen Garner had an idea to write a book about Australian rules football, her heart soared then immediately sank. entries.content:
A few years ago, when Helen Garner had an idea to write a book about Australian rules football, her heart soared then immediately sank. The impetus was Ambrose, her teenage grandson, who played for a local team. Garner enjoyed watching them and wanted to put this into writing. Then the dreary thought: “I’ll have to swot, read the rulebook.” People to whom she mentioned the idea assumed she’d be writing a polemic, “like what it means in society and how terrible it is and what violence means. And I’m going: ‘What a bore.’”

As anyone familiar with Garner’s almost 50-year writing career will know, there is nothing more igniting to the 83-year-old than the invitation to outrun boredom by going off in an unauthorised direction. Garner, who is speaking to me via video call from her home in Melbourne, occupies that tiny category of writers famous enough to be recognised in public. Stopped by strangers in the street, she’s often treated to their strong views about her work. As a result, perhaps, she has perfected a very Garnerian obstinacy, enabling her to resist other people’s bossy opinions which, in the case of The Season, meant no tedious explainers about the rules, history or sociology of Aussie rules football. Instead, says Garner, she envisaged following a single season of Ambrose’s U16s team, the Flemington Colts, as “a nanna’s book”. During publicity, she’d turn up to an event at a library to find “the first five rows packed with nannas; all these white-haired women with hankies in their hands. And I feel nobody writes about nannas. I mean, sentimentally, yes; but I want to say what they’re really like.”

To say what something is really like is the ethos behind all of Garner’s books and it has, on occasion, landed her in spectacular trouble. It has also won levels of devotion from readers who have turned her into an almost guru-like figure in her 80s, turbocharged by the publication last year of her wisdom-heavy diaries – which won the Baillie Gifford prize – and helped, one suspects, by her ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth. (A classic example: referring to the controversy around The First Stone, the 1995 book she wrote about feminism, Garner says: “I gave a lot of people the shits.” It’s not a line one can imagine, say, Marilynne Robinson delivering.)

The current mania around Garner is a long-overdue correction for a writer who, outside Australia, was ignored and condescended to for decades. In 1987, in a typically sniffy reference to Garner in the TLS, her work was referred to as “Mills& Boon for bohemians”, yet she is now credibly hailed as a contender for the Nobel prize, can fill 900-seat venues in New York, and has seen practically her entire back catalogue reissued in the US. (Carrie Bradshaw was shown carrying a copy of Garner’s 2014 book, This House of Grief, in a scene from And Just Like That … and Dua Lipa interviewed her on her podcast.) All of which Garner shrugs off, referring to herself as an “old kind of warhorse” who was never interested in prizes in the first place, not least, she says, because “you have to put on that look that you’re pleased for the other person”, even when – a typically bracing admission – “their book was not as good as mine”.

The fact is that Garner has always cut through the flab and waffle of so much literary culture in pursuit of something more honest. In her first novel, Monkey Grip, published in 1977 and based on her rackety life at the time, Garner told the story of Nora, a woman with a young child living in a bohemian shared house in Melbourne and on-off dating a heroin addict called Javo. Garner had arrived at this point in her own life partly as a result of fleeing a rigid, repressed childhood in the town of Geelong near Melbourne. As the oldest of six kids, she had frequently clashed with her father, a wool merchant and “a rather domineering person”, she says, who bullied her meek stay-at-home mother and kept no books in the house. After attending an Anglican girls’ school, Garner won a place at the University of Melbourne, where she spent the best part of three years in the pub. “It was a strange time. Once you get estranged from your parents, you go galumphing across the landscape seizing this and throwing out that. I look back and I see a lot of damage. We trampled through each other’s lives.”

This sense of damage would become more profound in Garner’s late 20s after a short-lived marriage to Bill Garner, whom she’d met at college and with whom she had a daughter, Alice. The pair split up when Alice was two and Garner moved into a series of hippy shared houses. It was an unstable life that had what Garner now calls a “kind of berserk quality to it – there was a lot of smashing and breaking that went on”, and only became more precarious when Garner, who had been working as a teacher, “opened my big mouth” and was fired from a school in Victoria for giving an impromptu and explicit sex education lesson. At the same time, she fell in love with a heroin addict and, a few years later, looking back over her diaries from that period, realised she wanted to write about it, embarking on Monkey Grip with the modest ambitions that enabled its fresh, uncontrived voice. “It was a private thing, writing down in a notebook what I thought about what was happening in my life,” she says. “So, I didn’t compare what I had written with anything great or mighty. I thought I’d just tell the story of what happened.”

Looking back now, she finds the novel “rather naive and undefended”. But it thrills her, 50 years on, that Monkey Grip is not only still in print, but highly popular. She was in a shop, recently, “and there was a young bloke who said: ‘Aren’t you Helen Garner? I’m reading Monkey Grip, and we’re living the life!’” She laughs and assumes a look of mock horror. “And I thought: ‘Ooh, don’t do that.’” I’d always assumed Javo had died way back, but fans of the book may be interested to know the real-life Javo is alive and well and living in Hobart, Tasmania, where he has a wife and grandchildren. After offering his spare room to Garner’s own 25-year-old grandchild who was visiting that part of the world recently, he wrote to Garner, “to say how marvellous it was to see our two grandchildren together”.

Monkey Grip, which was written with the electric, offhand energy of a young writer yet to grow self-conscious, caused a sensation in Australia and was followed by a series of short, brilliant novels, including The Children’s Bach and Cosmo Cosmolino, before Garner pivoted to nonfiction in the mid-1990s. (She’d return to fiction in 2008 with The Spare Room, based on Garner’s experience of nursing her close friend through cancer. The book has recently enjoyed an operatic adaptation in Melbourne.) And in the background, always, Garner maintained her diaries, recording her second marriage to Jean-Jacques Portail, a journalist whom she met in Paris, where she moved for a couple of years in the late 1970s while living on a writer’s grant and trying to write her second novel. Portail moved back to Melbourne with Garner, and they split up in 1985. A few years later, Garner moved to Sydney to be nearer to the writer Murray Bail, the man who would become her third and (to date) final husband, and who dominates the last volume of her diaries.

Alongside entries about fashion, art, friendship, nature and the end of her marriage to Bail, the diaries offer readers a chance to witness the epic battle between Garner’s extremely robust writer’s ego and its near-constant collapse. A typical entry, from 1997, reads: “I have to admit to myself that I feel irrelevant, small, hollow, untalented, worthless – and frightened. The energy required to maintain self-command is so great that I am always tired. How repellent one is. If only I were writing something.”

I’m curious about how Garner reconciles these two things – confidence and self-doubt – particularly in the wake of The First Stone, her first nonfiction book, in which she interrogated the case of two female students at the University of Melbourne who accused the master of their college of groping them. A mid-90s cause celebre in Australia, Garner foreshadowed culture wars to come by presenting the story as a possible overreaction on the part of the women, putting the boot in, she says, “to what I thought was a rather punitive form of feminism. I got into a hell of a lot of trouble. Really, it was quite astonishing, the amount of hostility I copped. I was thought to be a rotten feminist; a heretic. I heard that someone on a judging panel said: ‘If this book by Helen Garner even gets on the long list, I will’ … thunderous threats …’” Garner says: “I just laughed. Because I think it’s a sort of compliment.”

The First Stone was much more subtle and ambivalent than its detractors allowed, being a real intellectual reckoning with a complicated subject. Given the response, I’ve always wondered how Garner came back from it. “I had the shit kicked out of me! People savaged me. And it took me a while, but when I got over it, I thought: ‘Well, I survived that, and now I’m free. I can write what I really want. And I won’t have to see if it comes out pure.’ Being hated is very bracing. It’s not destructive. Well, it could be; if I’d published that book now … but the internet didn’t exist then. I did feel miserable and sad and I thought: ‘God, everyone hates me, this is terrible.’ But I didn’t regret it for a minute.”

Because it was the book you wanted to write? “Yeah. And I made mistakes in it; but I got a lot of amazing letters. I reckon I got about 800 and I answered every one. It was quite an exercise; someone would cover me with loathsome abuse and I’d write back: ‘Thank you for your kind letter …’ And the good letters I got were long and thoughtful, saying: ‘I read your book and I’d like to tell you something that happened to me.’ And that made me think I opened up the subject for people to talk about calmly.” It can’t have hurt that the book was a huge bestseller. “Yeah, and that really gave them the shits. And they’d go around saying: ‘Oh, yes, of course Helen’s motivation was purely commercial.’”

It helped that Garner had a career in freelance journalism to fall back on, particularly when she got stuck on a book, This House of Grief, which told the story of the trial and conviction of Robert Farquharson, who murdered his three children to get back at their mother, and which took eight years to finish while the various appeals played out. After the success of Monkey Grip, Garner dashed off a second novel, “and it was crap, and my publisher correctly bounced it back. That was a nasty moment, but they were right. Just because you’ve written one book doesn’t mean you know how to write the next one.” But while better novels followed, including The Children’s Bach, published in 1984 and widely considered her masterpiece, she moved permanently to nonfiction after The First Stone, coming to specialise in a kind of literary true crime with a series of devastating books built around high-profile murder trials.

That shift was brought about in part by her marriage to fellow novelist Murray Bail. Garner’s account of the collapse of that marriage appears in How to End a Story, her third volume of diaries, and it’s quite something; at one point, in a fury at the insidious, unfaithful Bail, she throws cups, an espresso machine and a saucepan full of beetroot soup across the kitchen. Garner writes that Bail belittled and gaslit her, and dismissed her work as inferior to his. “I thought my marriage was the worst marriage in the world and I was the world’s biggest wimp for going along with it,” she says. Since the diaries came out, however, a lot of people have said to her “‘that book is my marriage.’ And that sort of shocks me – they’re talking about a marriage they’re still in. But it can be terribly difficult. I reckon it’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kids.”

She regards having her only child, Alice – at the age of 26 and without any great planning – as the greatest good fortune of her life. And the happiest she has ever been, she says, has been during these past decades of living next door to Alice and her husband and three children. Bail, meanwhile, comes out of the diaries looking very bad indeed. Any feedback from him since publication? “The answer to that is no. And either he hasn’t read it or he’s saying he hasn’t read it. I haven’t had any contact with him now since long before I published the diaries. We parted badly and painfully and it’s never been mended.” She sighs. “He also published a memoir in which he summed up my part in his life in about three sentences. I was roundly dismissed. And I went on like it was the collapse of civilisation. But. You know. Bless him.”

Given the relative literary reputations of Helen Garner and Murray Bail these days, she can afford to be generous. And, of course, one of the delights of the diaries is the schadenfreude of watching a man flex his superiority over a woman who will, in time, be regarded as one of the great writers of our age. Splitting up gave her just the impetus she needed, she says. “I felt very liberated by no longer living in close companionship with someone who had ideas about literature which were too severe and didn’t suit my work. He had this hierarchy of forms, and I subscribed to them for a long time because I’d been educated to think that as well. But after I split up with him, I relaxed into being a nonfiction writer. And I stopped doing it defensively. I thought: ‘Actually, this is my natural form.’ And I still feel that very strongly: I’m out here, and I’m good at this, and it’s really fun to do, and it gets you out of the house, rather than stewing in your own self-hatred.”

So it was with The Season, in which for the space of winter training Garner showed up every week at the football ground to watch her grandson and his cohorts play. Garner went through her customary period of thinking it was all a mistake, that the book was a terrible idea and she’d never be able to drag it over the line. The toughest experience she ever had with this kind of self-doubt was during the writing of Joe Cinque’s Consolation, her deeply affecting 2004 book about the killing of Joe Cinque, a young engineer from New South Wales whose girlfriend injected him with ‘Get in there and do it!’ heroin and was later convicted of manslaughter. “I actually told Maria Cinque, his mother, that I wasn’t going to write the book. I wrote her a letter and said I’m really sorry, I’m going to have to give up, I can’t do this. And she rang me up and said: ‘What do you mean you can’t do it? We gave you our story, you said you were going to do it, you’ll do it! Do it!’ God, I nearly died of shame. I look back on that and think you need someone who’s going to kick you right up the arse. Don’t you think? You don’t want someone who’s going to say: ‘Oh, darling, it must be so hard, I really feel for you.’ You want someone to say: ”

This is Garner’s circuit, from idea to execution via collapse, shame and eventual, dogged persistence. A few days before our conversation, Anne Carson was announced as the winner of the Nobel Prize in literature, a decision thoroughly approved of by her Australian peer. Taped up on the wall of her office, Garner has a poem of Carson’s, which she looks at in times of dire need. “If I ever had a tattoo, I’d have that last line tattooed on me,” she says. “I just think it’s so marvellous.” The poem describes a stormy night at sea, fraught with peril, existential and otherwise. “And the last line is: ‘Nothing for it just row.’”

entries.title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October
entries.summary: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsI’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’s Like a Cat Loves a Bird was a winning blend of detail and readability. Continue reading...
entries.content:
Ian Rankin, author

I’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’s Like a Cat Loves a Bird was a winning blend of detail and readability.

A Bad, Bad Place by Frances Crawford is a prize-winning debut crime novel set in 1970s Glasgow. It’s clever, authentic and humane with unforgettable protagonists and pitch-black humour.

The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

David, Guardian reader

I’ve loved (most of) China Miéville’s books (I think that he and Alan Moore are the real doyens of “weird” fiction) – but The Rouse is surely his opus: sometimes prose-poetry, sometimes stream-of-consciousness, with shades (literally) of Lovecraft and MR James running through a bleak, unsettling yet compelling tale. I strongly suggest you take a very deep breath and launch into an adventure (lasting more than 1,200 pages) that will leave you dazed and amazed!

Louise Kennedy, author

I normally read one book at a time but, perhaps because I am on the road at the moment, I have three on the go. Emma Cline’s short story Arcadia almost killed me, and I’ve been a devotee ever since. Switzy, her new novel, accompanies on his final journey a man whose wealth and privilege offer no protection from the dementia that has begun to addle his poor brain. Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth: so far, charming, pretty Lily Bart is in charge of her story, but an encounter with a man who appears not to wish her well suggests there may be trouble ahead. John McGahern’s Memoir already has my heart rent in twain, to paraphrase an old Irish ballad, and he hasn’t even finished primary school.

Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Sophie, Guardian reader

Almost Life by Kiran Millwood Hargrave is a beautiful and heartbreaking love story that transported me back in time to Paris in the late 1970s and 80s. The main characters, Laure and Erica, as well as the other characters, soon feel like friends – friends who are human and imperfect, and who sometimes make frustrating decisions, but who are all the more lovable for it. It’s elegantly and smartly written, and paints such vivid pictures – I rarely read past my bedtime these days, but I stayed up late for this one, torn between wanting to finish and never wanting the book to end. It captures the feeling of love and being in love so well.

Mark, Guardian reader

This year, I’ve set myself the challenge of only reading books by writers who aren’t part of the Anglosphere, with each writer being from a different country. It’s certainly forced me to read stuff outside my comfort zone – which is how, this month, I’ve ended up reading Independent People by Halldór Laxness, a 500+ page novel about an Icelandic farming family. Over the course of about 20 years in the early 20th century, we follow the hardships and privations of a stubborn farmer who insists he fend for himself to maintain independence on his own land.

I expected this book to be unrelentingly grim reading – and in parts it is, especially in the almost indifference to death. But it’s also very humorous in its characters’ cynicism towards one another. It’s beautifully atmospheric in its prose, particularly the changing of the seasons and their effect on the dramatic landscape of the farm. Reading so much literature in translation has given me an appreciation of when it’s done well (without ever knowing the original text), and the translation by JA Thompson, in collaboration with Laxness, is sublime.

entries.title: Philippa Gregory: ‘I read 100 of the 18th century’s most popular novels – the perfect author’s apprenticeship’
entries.summary: The British novelist on discovering Molly Keane, coming to Dickens late, and the books that taught her the importance of writing about historyMy earliest reading memory My mother always read me a bedtime story, but by around age three, I was not looking at the pictures but reading the text. After that, I read to myself, and would read four books a week from the library.My favourite book growing up
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

My mother always read me a bedtime story, but by around age three, I was not looking at the pictures but reading the text. After that, I read to myself, and would read four books a week from the library.

My favourite book growing up

As a child I read Elizabeth Goudge’s The Little White Horse, and the combination of history and gothic fantasy was very powerful for me. It’s realistic and charming and frightening without being nightmarish. It started my love of historical fiction, and has since become a family favourite for my own children.

The book that changed me as a teenager

They all did, I was a voracious reader. I really enjoyed Rudyard Kipling, and later went on to historical fiction, especially Georgette Heyer. I read all of Jane Austen’s novels early on and learned to love her economy of style and precision. She still seems to me the finest writer in the English language.

The writer who changed my mind

EP Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class is a radical account of the emergence of a working-class consciousness and was a revelation to me when I first read it as a young woman. It made me understand the real importance of writing history, and the passion that a great historian can bring to the subject. It’s become a model for me in my own work – showing that you can find and write a hidden history.

The book that made me want to be a writer

For my PhD thesis I read more than 100 of the most popular novels in the 18th century. Don Quixote, Clarissa, Gulliver’s Travels, Moll Flanders and many more. It was the perfect author’s apprenticeship. Not only did I read the novels, I analysed them all, which meant I learned about structure, characterisation and tempo. But more importantly, I learned about the craft of novel writing at the very time novels were being invented.

The book I came back to

I didn’t enjoy Charles Dickens until later in life. Now, I think he is one of the great writers of the big book. One of my favourites of his is Dombey and Son. The huge sentimentalism around a beautiful frail child is combined with a story about a merciless social climber. It’s a great and unpredictable read.

The book I reread

Great writing gives any experience a significance, and a good novel can take us into another place and time. I read and reread Iris Murdoch’s The Sea, the Sea, whenever I need comfort. It’s a book that is far away from my own concerns and yet entirely about the human struggle to own the person you love, when you know that cannot be achieved, to free yourself from your own vanity and greed, to recognise those who are your deep companions and friends. At the same time it’s a deeply engaging story about a gossipy, vain theatre director in his retirement home at the sea.

The book I discovered later in life

I discovered Molly Keane, a between-the‑wars Anglo-Irish novelist, recently. At first sight she tells delicious stories of the eccentric Anglo-Irish wealthy elite, but every novel is highly aware of the injustice that underpins that society. One of my favourites is Good Behaviour, about a pair of adorable siblings who live for hunting in an enormous estate and care for nothing but each other, their horses and dogs, and their father, who they call “The Sir”. It’s a wonderful picture of a society that has completely disappeared, and a fictional creation of huge charm.

Royal Witch by Philippa Gregory is published by HarperCollins. To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup
entries.summary: Minihorror by Barbi Marković; Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch; Hafni Says by Helle Helle; Googling for Soul by Hamid IsmailovMinihorror by Barbi Marković, translated by Jen Calleja (Faber, £14.99) This eccentric and fantastical collection of very short stories is bursting with weird life. Mini and Miki (the Disney mouse names in Serbian) are a sometime boyfriend and girlfriend living in Austria. They
entries.content:
Minihorror by Barbi Marković, translated by Jen Calleja (Faber, £14.99)

This eccentric and fantastical collection of very short stories is bursting with weird life. Mini and Miki (the Disney mouse names in Serbian) are a sometime boyfriend and girlfriend living in Austria. They visit Mini’s family, who gather round a pit and make her climb down into it (when she told Miki “they’re dragging me down”, he thought it was a metaphor). They visit Miki’s family, where a dog Mini draws on a card comes alive and attacks her. Things swing from hopeful – “they’re having fun like a couple in an advert” – to dismal: a hair dye goes wrong and “Mini looks like a 13-year-old dog”. Minihorror combines a Bernhardian comic gloom (“in summary, everything’s tainted, and existence is a particular hardship”) with antic energy. “Miki isn’t sure what to think about life. Is it good? Is it bad?” It’s everything, just like this book.

Paradise Burns by Pol Guasch, translated by Mara Faye Lethem (Peninsula, £12.99)

“Stories, if you give them an order, aren’t stories but lies.” Catalan author Guasch makes the point vividly in this novel which flits briskly from present to past and from narrator to narrator. It’s set in a changed climate – “One only knows it’s winter now by the shrunken days and long nights” – where young men join a firefighting service and fight “wildfire simulations of blazes that could not be put out”. The central characters are friends Rita and Líton, but Líton is dead when the book begins – “twenty-four short years, a life as fleeting as a shooting comet” – so the story goes backward, to find out why. The jumpy narrative ranges from Rita’s childhood diary, to three “crafty old biddies” in the neighbourhood, to Líton and his lover René. But inside the hectic structure is a tribute to the value of friendship, and how a friend “has to be the net beneath the tightrope that is life”.

Hafni Says by Helle Helle, translated by Martin Aitken (Akoya, £12.99)

Hafni, at 48, is leaving her husband – literally, by taking a road trip through Denmark. “Many’s the time he’d cycle off and I’d be standing at the kitchen window wishing the wind would take him.” Now it’s her turn to go. Alongside details of life away from home – washing her pants in the sink, opening beer bottles with a metal comb – she reflects on how liberating it is to be free of a sense of obligation. The rules she has lived by can be abandoned, if not forgotten. “No more phrases like ‘you shouldn’t have’.” She meets new people – such as a dying woman who sees it as her duty to keep everyone around her cheerful – and wobbles between hope and fear. But ultimately this is a subtle, affecting story of what happens when a woman stuck in her life says, “I don’t want to be me. I want to change who I am.”

Googling for Soul by Hamid Ismailov, translated by Shelley Fairweather-Vega, Dani Ismailov, Irina Buss-Zolotareva and Andrew Bromfield (Glagoslav, £17.99)

This sequence of stories about Uzbeks, often exiled in Russia, is full of rampant action, blunt comedy and real horror. In the title story, a man believes his life is echoing the events of Andrey Platonov’s story Soul, and also believes that Hamid Ismailov, the author of this book, has been arrested on terrorism charges. (In reality, Ismailov was forced to flee Uzbekistan in 1992.) Other stories include a man driven to penury by the escapades of a nephew he’s never met before; two in-laws thrown together by fate; and a girl with a precious doll (her story seems more subdued than the others until her drunk father chases her with a knife). Ismailov’s characters have a lively line in insults: “You have the complexion of a fart,” says a father telling his son to eat better. “It’s as if the world had rejected seriousness,” says one character – but Ismailov’s blend of seriousness and sparkle is a seductive combination.

entries.title: Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s tale
entries.summary: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answersThe Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying
entries.content:
The Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying account of abuse in Lolita to the devastating misinterpretation at the heart of Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the trope of the unreliable narrator exposes the dangerous gap between the stories we tell and the truths they obscure. In Attention Seeking Behaviour, the reader is asked to examine their own capacity for trust.

A young woman aspires to be a writer – yet she has paused her postgraduate degree in poetry. She works unfulfilling jobs that demand little from her and has a lot of sex, which she describes as offering her “solitude”. She does all this while lying compulsively. She lies for fun, to flirt, to steal, for sympathy. She lies out of a desire to hurt others, but also to preserve her own privacy. Lying is, as the narrator claims, universal, though success at lying is not. She regards fraudsters and scammers with derision: they are “divorced from reality” and give her “second hand embarrassment”. In her eyes, her own lies are somehow purer.

Grief and trauma pulse beneath the story, as the narrator is haunted by the dead bodies she sees in parks and floating in canals. She says she has called emergency services, but her account is slippery: the harder we try to grasp it, the more it slips through our fingers. Can we believe a word she says?

Attention Seeking Behaviour draws the reader through personal confession and a gripping narrative of misadventures while dating, but the novel loses some of its momentum in its discussions of deceit. An essay on Paul Ekman’s Facial Action Coding System for classifying facial movements to determine deception disrupts the narrative drive. When this bleeds into the narrative, her boyfriend says: “No more. Please.” These sections interrupt the flow and lack the immediacy achieved elsewhere.

In the book’s second part, questions of credibility become more acute. Acting on behalf of a journalist, the narrator copies files at a legal firm relating to a rape case in which a lecturer is accused of assaulting his student. The victim bares her soul, giving first her phone over to the police, then her laptop. Eventually, after police question her for signs of deception, she withdraws her participation in the investigation. The case is closed.

Complainants often anticipate the difficulties of a police investigation. Their testimony is the evidence, their body a crime scene. The narrator says: “We are ambiently aware of what is believable – of what people think is true, whether or not it is real.” Victims of sexual violence are judged in courts and beyond, for what they wore on the night in question, for what they did or did not do in the aftermath. Here lies the book’s genius: it turns the question of reliability back on the reader, exposing the expectations we place on women. Must an account of rape be consistent, coherent or complete to be worthy of belief? Should a woman’s past, including what she has said and done, have any bearing on whether she is believed? The reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itself. The narrator cannot name the trauma that happened with her ex-boyfriend Isaac. Instead, she unravels it “like a police report”, recounting what she said (nothing) and what she felt (numb). The book asks, unflinchingly, do you believe her?

Brilliant and breathless, Attention Seeking Behaviour brings no easy resolutions to questions of memory, truth and justice. Yet, as the narrator tells us again and again, all she wants is to be believed.

entries.title: ‘We sold out tickets within 13 minutes’: new novel from romantasy author Sarah J Maas sparks fan mania
entries.summary: Move over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge salesWhen The Spicy Librarian, a romance bookshop in Leamington Spa, announced a masquerade ball to celebrate the new Sarah J Maas novel, 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets. “We sold out within 13 mi
entries.content:
When The Spicy Librarian, a romance bookshop in Leamington Spa, announced a masquerade ball to celebrate the new Sarah J Maas novel, 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets. “We sold out within 13 minutes,” says the shop’s co-founder Ali Maynard James. “As soon as tickets went on sale, our website crashed”.

The shop was one of many across the UK marking the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, the first instalment of Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series in more than five years. On Monday night, bookshops threw parties and opened past midnight – and The Spicy Librarian hired a stately home to mark the occasion.

The book, the sixth in the series known to fans as Acotar, went on sale at 12.01am on Tuesday. Few releases carry as much commercial weight – the first book, a dark retelling of Beauty and the Beast, was published in 2015, with later books following the adventures of Feyre across the faerie lands of Prythian. By 2021 the series had sold 13m copies, and across her three interlinked fantasy series, Maas has now sold more than 75 m books in 40 languages.

The Spicy Librarian, which bills itself as Europe’s largest independent romance bookshop, held its ball at Ragley Hall in Warwickshire, where riders dressed as “fae warriors” carried torches on horseback. Tickets were £149 – the shop ran the event again the following night, which also sold out, and ordered about 750 copies to cover both balls and its pre-orders.

“We gave everyone the books at midnight, and people started reading them immediately,” says Maynard James. “Some people stayed up and devoured the whole thing in a few hours.”

Maas is the biggest name in romantasy, a genre combining fantasy and romance which has grown from an online niche into one of publishing’s most lucrative categories. Last year, Onyx Storm by Rebecca Yarros – another romantasy star – had the biggest first week for a hardback novel in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015. In 2024, booming sales of romance and fantasy helped push UK fiction revenue above £1bn for the first time. The genre’s readers are largely young women, and much of its growth has played out on TikTok.

“It’s been such a long wait for this book, people are just itching to get their hands on it,” says Starlin Marot, owner of Bad Girl Books in Oxford, the UK’s first romantasy-only bookshop. “For so many of us, the series has been like a gateway drug into the genre, or into reading itself.”

In Oxford, Marot had only planned to open Bad Girl Books for half an hour after midnight, for a couple of readers who had asked on Instagram. Instead, a queue formed outside. “It was just crazy, like a flurry of people came in,” she says. “I was honestly not expecting that many people just for half an hour. But it shows how popular these books are!”

Her midnight release doubled as a pyjama party. “It was cute and cosy vibes,” Marot says. “We had Acotar-themed cakes and drinks.”

In London, romance bookshop Main Character Books decided against a midnight opening, serving breakfast to readers collecting pre-orders instead and holding an evening party for 45 people. “We decorated the entire store,” says owner Cassie Simmons. “In early October we had more pre-orders than we expected … we doubled our order at the publisher.” After Tuesday’s sales, the shop ordered again. “We’re going through stock even faster than we expected.”

The latest book is the first part of a four-part story. A Court of Forgotten Melody, out on 12 January, contains the next two parts, and the last is still being written.

“I think it’s definitely the five-year wait and the hype that’s been going up online,” says Simmons.

Maynard James, who says Acotar got her reading for pleasure again after becoming a mother, believes its heroines are a big part of the draw for its largely female fanbase. “They aren’t women that are damsels in distress that need rescuing or saving,” she says. “They almost prioritise themselves before they prioritise love. We want the women to be the centre of their own story.”

For the specialist shops, the boom is showing up in the till. “Sales are so much higher than I even anticipated for the year already,” says Marot. “It’s so exciting.”

While a Hulu adaptation of Acotar was announced in 2021, Maas has now bought back rights. “I want to see everything adapted the way I envision it, and the way I know fans want it”, she said in March.

entries.title: Sarah Howe wins Forward poetry prize for best collection
entries.summary: Howe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categoriesSarah Howe has won the Forward prize for best collection, one of the UK’s most prestigious poetry awards, for Foretokens, a collection that explores new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother’s early life in Hong Kong.Howe was announced as the win
entries.content:
Sarah Howe has won the Forward prize for best collection, one of the UK’s most prestigious poetry awards, for Foretokens, a collection that explores new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother’s early life in Hong Kong.

Howe was announced as the winner during a ceremony hosted by Joelle Taylor at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday evening, and will receive £10,000.

Howe was born in Hong Kong to an English father and a Chinese mother. Foretokens, her second collection, comes a decade after Loop of Jade became the first debut to win the TS Eliot prize. Foretokens was also shortlisted for the 2025 TS Eliot prize.

Reviewing Foretokens for the Guardian, Rishi Dastidar called it “a quite brilliant return”, praising Howe’s “keen, probing intelligence”. “Taking on the biggest of subjects – genetics, time’s relativity, becoming a parent – as well as re-examining her mother’s occluded history in Hong Kong, there is now an anger in Howe’s tonal range, which brings a pleasing sharpness to her investigations,” he wrote.

The Forward prizes’ co-executive director, Mónica Parle, described Foretokens as “an exceptional collection” that “can emerge after 10 years in the making and still bear distinct relevance to our time”.

The prize also recognised three other winners. Nur Turkmani, a Lisbon-based poet who grew up in Beirut, won the £5,000 Jerwood prize for best first collection for October, which was also shortlisted for this year’s PEN Heaney prize. The poems were mostly written in Beirut during a period when “there were protests, wildfires, economic collapse, a port explosion and an ongoing war”, Turkmani said, “and writing became a way of seeing, understanding and continuing”. It is the first nomination and first win for her publisher, the independent Hajar Press.

The Dublin-born poet Tara Bergin, who teaches creative writing at Newcastle University, won the Forward prize for best single poem in written form for The Fear, first published in the Irish literary magazine the Stinging Fly. “Many years ago I devised a poetry writing class called ‘Fear Poetry’,” she said. “I got so interested in the whole idea I had to try it myself.”

The Scottish singer-songwriter Biff Smith, who won both the Scottish and World Poetry Slam Championships last year, received the prize for best single poem in the performance category for Dumbarton East, recorded at the Scottish performance night Loud Poets. Smith wrote the poem on a train: “So much of life is spent in transit, I feel an urge to make that time count – do some knitting, learn Italian or whatever (maybe even write a poem).” Bergin and Smith each received £1,000.

This year’s judges were the novelist Sarah Moss, who chaired the panel, alongside Romalyn Ante, WN Herbert, Michael Mullen and Yomi Ṣode. “In months when the world could easily seem darker every week, it was consoling to be called back into poems and collections and performances day after day,” said Moss, “not because poetry is any kind of panacea but because poets give us words, images and metaphors for what matters in interesting times.”

The Forward prizes were established in 1992 and have recognised some of the biggest names in poetry, including Seamus Heaney, Ted Hughes and Claudia Rankine. Last year, the best collection prize was shared for the first time in its history, between Vidyan Ravinthiran for Avidyā and Karen Solie for Wellwater.

  • Foretokens by Sarah Howe (Vintage Publishing, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: War Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three?

entries.content:
Are we on the brink of a new world war? This bleak subject is increasingly invoked by leaders, soldiers and officials, from Donald Trump to Vladimir Putin to the heads of our military and intelligence services. It’s an urgent theme, then, for the FT foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman to explore in his latest survey of global diplomacy. Rachman draws his title from the expression, sometimes attributed to Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” – the idea being that conflict doesn’t much care whether we like to think about it or not: it will come knocking on our doors regardless.

Clearly, humanity is in a particularly unsafe spot right now, but seeing our security issues laid out like this, catalogued and mapped and analysed, they seem almost overwhelming. To summarise: the most powerful, nuclear-armed states – the US, China and Russia – are led by unscrupulous, self-dealing “strongmen”, each of whom is playing with the nationalist “Great Again” politics epitomised by Trump. Democracy is being rolled back around the world, and even bastions of liberalism such as the UK, France and Germany seem vulnerable to takeover by the Putin-friendly far right. The so-called rules-based international order and its institutions – the UN, the WTO, Nato – are being deliberately undermined by the aforementioned strongmen, and are as weak now as they have ever been.

Putin has described the new world order with the term “might makes right”, and the result is that conflicts have been breaking out at a rate unprecedented in the postwar era. According to Rachman, there were 61 in 2024 alone, and 11 full-blown wars. This included Gaza as well as some conflicts far less visible in the west, such as the one in Sudan, which by mid-2025 had led to 150,000 battlefield deaths. In 2026 many “state-based conflicts” are ongoing, including the largest land war in Europe since 1945 (in Ukraine) and the most disruptive in the Middle East for more than 20 years (Iran). Although these are mostly confined to their regions, they have begun to overlap and spread, as Russia deploys North Korean troops and tests Nato’s resolve, Iran throttles global shipping, and Ukraine advises Gulf states on drone use. And even as these grind on, others threaten to explode, including between India and Pakistan, North and South Korea, and China and Taiwan.

Of these potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world war, since it could bring China and the US into direct conflict. For decades, Taiwan’s security was guaranteed by US naval superiority; now Beijing, after a massive military buildup, has more warships than Washington. It’s said that the single Chinese shipyard on Changxing Island has more capacity than all US yards combined. Still, Xi Jinping knows that if the US comes to Taiwan’s aid, the result would be a bloodbath, which is why US presidents have mostly been keen to emphasise the US’s commitment to Taiwan. But Trump has been far more ambivalent – declaring in May this year, for instance, that “I think the last thing we need right now is a war that’s 9,500 miles away” – which only increases the risk of China attempting an assault.

It’s here, in the shifting power balance between China and the US, that the root of the new global insecurity lies. Whatever you think of American hegemony, the US maintained a sort of stability, after the cold war, in which victims could plausibly appeal to international law. The 2003 invasion of Iraq destroyed that system, and US failure there and in Afghanistan persuaded future presidents against intervention. Three times, between 2012 and 2015, Obama chose not to step in to address illegal acts by the Assad regime, Russia and China, which signalled an American retrenchment. The Trump administration has taken this further, reverting to the kind of isolationist, tariff-based protectionism that postwar institutions such as the UN security council and WTO were built to avoid. It’s hard not to spot echoes here of the 1930s – the time, incidentally, when the slogan “America first” was popularised.

How to offset these risks? Rachman surveys a handful of mechanisms that have helped maintain the peace, and finds them wanting. The rules-based international order, for instance, barely functioned in its heyday; now, as Mark Carney put it plainly, it “no longer works”: we are living through a “rupture”. What about spreading democracy and economic stability as a path to peace – a principle exemplified by the “Golden Arches” theory, which states that no two nations with McDonald’s will wage war on each other? There’s no comfort here either, as that was proved wrong in the 1990s, and the number of democracies has been declining steadily since 2006. Then there’s deterrence, which still by and large keeps us safe. But it hasn’t stopped fighting between nuclear-armed India and Pakistan, and China and North Korea are rapidly expanding their atomic arsenals.

What we’re left with, then, as American primacy declines, is a global version of Trump’s “Donroe doctrine”, in which each major power gets a “sphere of influence” where they call the shots. In this scenario, Washington rules over the Americas, Beijing over east Asia, and Moscow the old Soviet zone. Clashes are sorted out by one-to-one conversations between authoritarian leaders. But what if these rulers fall out? And anyway, who wants to live in the shadow of an overbearing neighbour?

While the outlook of War Is Interested in You is undoubtedly gloomy, Rachman’s book is not. His writing is engaging and anecdotal, and he brings vast experience to bear on a vital subject. He won’t go so far as to say a new world war is inevitable, but the threat is becoming impossible to ignore.
